title: Systematic errors from scalar slowing-down models in transient SERF magnetometry
authors: Marek Kopciuch, Harini Raghavan, Morgan W. Mitchell
abstract: Reduced Bloch models of spin-exchange-relaxation-free (SERF) magnetometers commonly describe the coupled electron--nuclear spin dynamics using a single nuclear slowing-down factor. We show that this scalar description becomes inaccurate when the polarization magnitude changes appreciably. We derive an effective Bloch equation with separate longitudinal and transverse slowing-down factors, $q_\parallel(P)$ and $q_\perp(P)$, governing changes in polarization magnitude and direction. For $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ under representative SERF conditions and undergoing free-induction decay (FID), comparison with master-equation simulations shows that the dynamic scalar model produces a magnetic-field estimation bias of up to $4.2\%$ at high initial polarization, while fixing the slowing-down factor at a reference value increases the error to $10.1\%$. Lowering the polarization suppresses this bias but also reduces the magnetic-field information contained in the FID signal. We further show that the anisotropic response modifies noncollinear optical pumping and introduces an additional nonlinear contribution to the harmonic response under periodic driving. The resulting model retains the simplicity of a three-component Bloch description while improving the quantitative accuracy of transient and driven SERF magnetometry.
summary: This paper analyzes systematic errors in SERF magnetometry arising from oversimplified models of spin dynamics. The authors show that treating the spin slowing-down factor as a single scalar quantity is inaccurate when polarization changes. They derive a more accurate, anisotropic Bloch equation using separate longitudinal and transverse factors, significantly improving the quantitative precision of magnetic field measurements.
main_problem: The conventional scalar description of spin slowing-down factors in SERF magnetometry becomes inaccurate when the polarization magnitude changes significantly.
main_result: The authors derive an anisotropic Bloch equation using separate longitudinal and transverse slowing-down factors, which significantly improves the quantitative accuracy of magnetic-field estimation compared to scalar models.
method: The analysis involves deriving an effective Bloch equation from a full master equation by retaining separate longitudinal and transverse slowing-down factors, $q_{\parallel}(P)$ and $q_{\perp}(P)$.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Spin-Exchange-Relaxation-Free (SERF) magnetometers using alkali-metal vapors, specifically ${}^{87}	ext{Rb}$. The dynamics are modeled using an anisotropic Bloch equation derived from a master equation.
key_observables: Magnetic-field estimation bias, polarization magnitude ($P$), and the separate slowing-down factors ($q_{\parallel}(P)$ and $q_{\perp}(P)$).
important_parameters: High initial polarization ($P_0$), temperature ($T$), and the degree of polarization change during the measurement.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption being challenged is the validity of the scalar approximation, which assumes the evolution only rotates the polarization vector rather than changing its magnitude.
figures_summary: Figure 5 shows the nuclear slowing-down factors ($q_{\perp}$ and $q_{\parallel}$) versus electron polarization ($P$) for various isotopes. Figure 2 compares the magnetic-field estimation bias across different model approximations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the inadequacy of the scalar model to deriving the full anisotropic Bloch equation, quantifying the resulting systematic biases (up to 10.1% error), and concluding that the anisotropic model maintains simplicity while improving accuracy for transient and driven measurements.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses systematic errors in high-precision quantum sensing platforms (SERF magnetometers) by refining the underlying quantum dynamics model, which is crucial for extracting accurate physical parameters from measured signals.

The master- equation reference is compared with the anisotropic, dynamic scalar, and fixed scalar (qref = 6) models over a 15 ms inter- val. All Bloch curves neglect the nuclear Zeeman correction. Simulation details are listed in Appendix C.

FIG. 2. Precession angle bias and magnetic-field informa- tion versus initial polarization. (a) Relative accumulated- precession bias bϕ for the anisotropic, dynamic scalar, and fixed scalar (q = 6) models, with colors as in Fig. 1. The ad- ditional dashed curve includes the nuclear Zeeman correction in the anisotropic model. (b) Master-equation Fisher infor- mation normalized to its maximum. (c) Residual bias of the nuclear-corrected anisotropic model at the temperatures indi- cated in the boxes. A transverse field of 5 nT is applied after preparation. Simulation details are listed in Appendix C.

FIG. 3. Analytical amplitude-precession maps for 87Rb at γeB⊥/RSD = 1. (a) Precession angle ϕsc shared by the dy- namic and fixed scalar models. (b) Anisotropy correction ∆ϕan = ϕan −ϕsc, where ϕan is the anisotropic-model preces- sion. (c) Nuclear Zeeman correction ∆ϕnuc = ϕan+nuc −ϕan. To keep the color scales readable, both P and P0 are sampled between 0.01 and 1, retaining only P ≤P0.
